newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU orders Spain to open telecoms sector.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU orders Spain to open telecoms sector.

text.p: The European Commission, under pressure at the WTO telecoms talks in Geneva, has firmly told the Spanish government that it must open its telecommunications sector to fair competition from January 1, 1998.
This is the date agreed for the full liberalisation of the sector in all but a few smaller EU states.
It also insisted that Spain start granting telecoms licences in the first half of 1998, which is the only way of ensuring effective competition.

"(European Competition Commissioner Karel) Van Miert wishes Spain to confirm rapidly its readiness to renounce (a five-year delay) and commit itself formally to the date of January 1, 1998 regarding full liberalisation of services and infrastructure," the Commission said in a statement.

The issue, which has been poisoning relations between Madrid and the Commission for about a year, holds the key to the EU's clearance of a joint venture between four European operators, including Telefonica de Espana SA, and AT&T Corp.

The opening of the Spanish telecoms market, Europe's fifth largest, is also crucial for the Union's position in the talks at the World Trade Organisation on bringing down national barriers in the fast-growing telecoms sector.

"Spain has...a particular significance in the WTO negotiations given the size of its domestic market and the presence of its dominant operator (Telefonica) in several Latin American countries," the statement said.

After the Commission discussed the issue at its regular meeting this week, Van Miert wrote a letter to the Spanish government asking for quick confirmation that it will stick to the 1998 deadline. The letter also insists that Madrid commit itself to granting licences to new telecoms operators during the first half od 1998.
The move is further proof that the Commission will not compromise on the 1998 date, despite a five-year delay won by Spain during tough Union negotiations on telecoms liberalisation in the early 80s.

It is in a strong position because it can use its power to vet the Unisource joint venture between the Swiss, Dutch, Swedish and Spanish telecoms operators as leverage. Unisource has concluded a global alliance with AT&T which the Commission is also examining.
The Spanish government has been fighting for the right to protect its market at least until mid 1999.
Commission sources said that the latest offer presented by Spanish minister in charge of telecommunications Rafael Arias Salgado was to grant licences by October 1999.

The EU's smaller states also have the right to delay breaking national telecoms monopolies and have recently asked the Commission to confirm that right. They are Ireland, Portugal, Luxembourg and Greece.
